title: Introduction to SQL
subtitle: What databases are, why SQL exists, and how tables work
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Applications need to store, retrieve, and update large amounts of structured data reliably. Files don't scale — searching a 10 GB text file for a user is impractical.
whyItExists.solution: A relational database stores data in tables (rows and columns), indexes it for fast lookup, and lets you query it with SQL — a declarative language readable by humans and computers.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time your data is structured, relational, and needs to be queried, filtered, sorted, or aggregated. Every serious application has a database.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For unstructured data (images, videos), use blob storage. For document-heavy workloads, consider MongoDB. For time-series, InfluxDB. For caches, Redis. SQL is still used alongside all of these.

explainModes.beginner: A database is like a spreadsheet that a computer can search instantly. Each sheet is a table. Each row is a record (one person, one order). Each column is a field (name, email, price). SQL is the language you use to ask questions — 'give me all users from Delhi'.
explainModes.simple: Database: a file managed by a database engine (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL). Table: rows + columns, like a spreadsheet. Schema: the blueprint — column names and types. Primary key: a unique ID for every row. Foreign key: a column that references another table's primary key. SQL: Structured Query Language — the standard language for all relational databases.
explainModes.standard: Relational databases enforce data integrity through constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY). Data is normalised to avoid duplication — a user appears once in the users table, referenced by ID elsewhere. The database engine handles storage, indexing, transactions, and concurrent access. SQL is declarative — you describe WHAT you want, not HOW to get it. The engine figures out the execution plan.
explainModes.technical: Relational model (Codd, 1970): data as mathematical relations. SQL = DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) + DML (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) + DCL (GRANT/REVOKE) + TCL (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK). ACID guarantees: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. B-tree indexes for fast range scans. Hash indexes for exact lookups. EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE for query plan inspection.
explainModes.deepDive: The relational model's mathematical foundation is relational algebra (selection σ, projection π, join ⋈). SQL optimisers use cost-based optimization — statistics about table sizes and column distributions to choose join order and index usage. WAL (Write-Ahead Log) for crash recovery. MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) for isolation without locking reads. Modern databases add JSON columns, full-text search, and geospatial types to the relational foundation.

content.text: A relational database stores data in tables. Each table has columns (defining what data is stored) and rows (actual records). Tables can reference each other via keys — that's the 'relational' part.

content.definition: A named grid of rows (records) and columns (fields). Like a spreadsheet tab, but with strict types and constraints.
A column (or combination) that uniquely identifies every row. Usually an auto-incrementing integer: id = 1, 2, 3, ...
A column that stores the primary key of a row in another table. orders.user_id references users.id — linking each order to the user who placed it.

content.text: Throughout this SQL course, we'll use a simple e-commerce database with three tables. Every interactive playground in every lesson has these tables pre-loaded.

content.code:
-- users: people who have accounts
users(id, name, email, city, joined_at)

-- products: items for sale
products(id, name, category, price, stock)

-- orders: purchases (links users to products)
orders(id, user_id, product_id, quantity, total, ordered_at)

questions.question: What does a primary key do?
options: Uniquely identifies each row in a table
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row — no two rows can have the same primary key value. It's how you refer to a specific record. Foreign keys in other tables reference primary keys to create relationships between tables.

faq.q: What is the difference between SQL and a database?
faq.a: SQL is a language — it's like Python or JavaScript. A database is a program that stores data — like SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. You use SQL to communicate with any of these databases. The same SQL (mostly) works across all of them.

SQLite for learning, prototyping, and small apps (no setup needed — it's a single file). PostgreSQL for production web apps. MySQL/MariaDB for legacy stacks. This course teaches standard SQL that works everywhere, with notes on differences.

examples: Every Django/Rails/Laravel app uses a SQL database as its primary data store
SQLite is the most deployed database in the world — it's in every phone and browser
Data analysts use SQL daily to query databases for reports and dashboards
